"No experience, how do I prove I can do it?"

This is a problem many fresh graduates face when job hunting. Seeing a job posting aimed at newcomers that also says "relevant experience preferred, able to get up to speed quickly," it's natural to worry: to gain experience, you need a job first; to get a job, you need to prove you have experience. Just this circular logic is discouraging enough.

In the past, newcomers often started by getting familiar with work through small tasks: organizing materials, recording discussions, checking spreadsheets, writing first drafts. They'd work slowly at first and make mistakes, but someone would point out what was wrong. After doing it a few times, people gradually understood one thing: what information matters, what results can be delivered, who to confirm with when problems arise.

Now, AI can organize materials first, transcribe recordings, draft copy. It's taking over some tasks, but this will change where newcomers start learning. If teams hand all simple tasks to tools without arranging new practice and mentoring, newcomers might face a real problem: before they've had time to learn basic work, they're being asked to deliver mature results directly.

This concern can also be seen in domestic fresh graduate surveys. 51job launched a fresh graduate special survey in May 2026, receiving 6,352 company questionnaires and 18,792 individual questionnaires. Among surveyed fresh graduates, 35.9% feel AI has replaced some traditional positions, 30.2% feel AI has brought new positions, and 26.7% feel the number of positions hasn't changed much but capability requirements have changed. Companies' answers are different: 68.3% believe overall staffing needs are roughly stable, mainly with some position adjustments; those who believe basic positions are being replaced and fresh graduate demand is decreasing account for 7.3%.

These numbers aren't saying how much fresh graduate positions nationwide have decreased. Students are talking about what they personally feel, companies are talking about how overall staffing needs are changing—they're not talking about the same thing. But this gap is worth noting: companies might feel total headcount hasn't changed significantly, but job seekers already feel "it's harder to get in, requirements are higher."

Job advertisements also show work opportunities are changing. PwC's analysis of mainland China recruitment information shows that in 2025, AI application positions increased by nearly 90,000, a year-on-year growth of 50.8%; AI development positions increased by about 30,500, a year-on-year growth of 15.5%. This is talking about AI-related positions, not that newcomer positions in all industries are increasing, nor does it prove AI application positions are fresh graduate positions. At least, it shows the market needs not just people who develop models, but also positions that apply AI to actual work.

Don't Guess "What the Company Wants," Look at What They're Actually Hiring For

Many people, when anxious, start chasing the latest tools, memorizing prompts, thinking that as long as they write "proficient in using AI" on their resume, they'll have a bit more opportunity. But what recruiters usually want to know is: can you complete specific things in this job?

Instead of preparing by feeling, choose a position you want to apply for, go to recruitment websites to look at real positions. For example, select city and position name, write down the 20 most recent job postings you've seen. This number is just a small sample for your own observation, not representing the entire industry. Focus on three things:

  • What does the work involve daily? Circle the action words in the job description: organize, follow up, analyze, communicate, produce, check—which ones appear repeatedly?
  • How does the employer judge if you can do it? Record the experience, portfolio, software, or industry knowledge they require. Distinguish between "must have" and "nice to have," don't assume everyone needs to know everything just from one job posting.
  • Which tasks can you practice yourself? Find a small task that can be completed with public materials, don't touch internal company data, and don't do real projects for the company for free.

After looking at these job postings, you'll get a more specific question than "will AI replace me": for the type of work I want to do, what's the most common and most worth practicing task first?

Make a Small Sample, Turn "I Can" Into a Visible Process

Suppose you want to do new media operations. If job postings repeatedly mention topic selection, content organization, data observation, pick one of these tasks and do a small practice yourself: choose a public account, record what recent content is about and who it's aimed at, then write a suggestion for how you would improve it.

AI can help you summarize content, and can help you polish expression. But you need to leave your own judgment: why did you choose these samples? What information supports your conclusion? Did AI get the content wrong? What did you delete or change in the end? If the suggestion is to be implemented, what information is needed next?

Organize it into one page: what the task was, where the materials came from, how you did it, which step AI helped with, what you checked and changed, and what you delivered in the end. In an interview, don't just say "I've used AI," you can tell a complete process: what problem I received, how I found materials, what I discovered, why I handled it this way.

If you want to do administration, sales, design, or other work, you can use the same method, but the practice content should be selected from the job postings you're looking at. This operations example in the text is just demonstrating the method, not saying all operations positions need to do the same thing.

This kind of practice can't replace formal work experience, nor can it guarantee getting an interview. Its use is more basic: instead of just handing over a resume that says "strong learning ability," you can take out a small thing you've done, showing the interviewer how you think, how you verify, and how you finish things.

There's also a boundary to maintain: use public materials for practice, clearly mark sources; don't upload personal information, company materials, or unpublished documents to AI; and don't present practice as real client projects. If a recruiter asks you to complete a large real task that can be directly used for free, that's already more than just a capability test, first think clearly whether the investment is worth it.

What You Can Really Accumulate Is the Ability to Finish Things

AI can make the first draft faster, but it can't take responsibility for results for you. Whether materials are reliable, whether numbers are read correctly, whether suggestions answer the question, whose confirmation is still needed before delivery—these still need human judgment. Newcomers used to learn these by doing small tasks, now they can also proactively find opportunities to practice, just the practice needs to be more conscious, and the process needs to be documented.

This doesn't mean every young person must become an AI expert. For many positions, doing one specific job well is more convincing than lining up a row of tool names on a resume. Asking questions is the start; being able to check answers, find errors, and explain your choices is what lets others see you're ready to take on work.

If you're preparing to send out resumes, today pick a target position, open 20 related job postings, find a task that appears repeatedly. Use public materials to make a small sample, write down how you did it, how you checked it, and why you made changes.

It won't magically become your years of work experience. But when an interviewer asks "you don't have experience, how do you prove you can do it," at least you can put forward a real thing you've done and clearly explain how you completed it.

When you were looking for your first job, what was the hardest part to get through? If you're already in the industry, what small thing made you first feel "I can do this job"? Welcome to share your experience in the comments. Your experience might be able to help someone who's still looking for that first step.

If you have people around you who are also looking for their first job, you can share this with them and talk about what small thing they're planning to start with.

When will AI surpass human experts? This question, insiders have finally given a clear timeline.

OpenAI co-founder and RLHF technology leader John Schulman's latest prediction: AI may comprehensively surpass top human experts in 3-4 years.

3-4 years. Not 30 years, not 10 years, but a time scale you and I can still clearly perceive.

I'm Shanshan, a 50-year-old AI observer. Today I won't sell anxiety, just break this down to look at it—after seeing clearly, you might actually feel less panicked.

I. AI Evolution Speed Has Already Surpassed Imagination

Let's look at a few numbers first to feel this speed.

Claude-generated code already accounts for over 80% of merged codebases. Per-engineer output has reached 8 times that of 2024. AI's independent task execution duration has broken through 16 hours, roughly doubling every 4 months.

What does this mean? It means AI is no longer at the level of "helping you look up information," it's already doing complete work that requires long periods of focus.

Schulman now works at Thinking Machines, researching a direction that sounds a bit scary—recursive self-improvement (RSI). Simply put, it's letting AI improve itself.

The RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) technology he led is the core of what makes ChatGPT "understand human language." This person is now researching letting AI self-evolve without needing human feedback.

If RSI succeeds, AI's progress speed will no longer be limited by human feedback speed.

II. Expert Internal Predictions Vary Greatly

But interestingly, top experts' internal judgments on this timeline vary shockingly.

Schulman gives 3-4 years. Another OpenAI co-founder O'Neill gives 5-10 years. Millidge gives 5 years.

Equally frontline participants, predictions differ by over 5 years.

Why such a big difference? Because there's a core bottleneck no one can avoid:

AI doesn't know "what goals to pursue."

Technically, AI can run faster and faster. But "which direction to run" and "what level counts as good"—these questions are still being defined by humans.

Schulman himself said something very clear: "Defining 'what we actually want' will be humanity's last bastion."

This sentence is worth middle-aged people contemplating carefully.

III. Middle-Aged People Don't Need to Panic, But Need to See Three Things Clearly

3-4 years, AI might surpass top experts. So what should ordinary people do? What should middle-aged people do?

My judgment: no need to panic, but need to see three things clearly.

First: Don't compete with AI on execution speed, amplify judgment ability.

AI writes code faster than you, makes PPTs faster than you, analyzes data faster than you. These things you can't compete on, and don't need to.

But what AI can't do is: judge whether this project should be done, judge whether this risk should be avoided, judge what this client's real needs are.

Industry insight, risk judgment, understanding of human nature—these are things middle-aged people have accumulated over 20+ years, things AI won't learn in the short term.

Second: Use AI well, but distinguish boundaries.

Research, writing first drafts, organizing data—hand these to AI. Direction, risks, decisions—keep these for yourself.

AI is a tool, not a boss. You use it to increase efficiency, but can't let it make decisions for you.

What's really valuable isn't "knowing how to use AI," but "knowing when not to use AI."

Third: Maintain the ability to try.

Try 1-2 new AI tools each month, not to become an expert, but to maintain curiosity and adaptability.

For a 50-year-old, the scariest thing isn't not knowing how to use AI, but "not wanting to learn new things." Once you stop trying, you're really left behind by the times.

IV. A 50-Year-Old's Perspective: The Real Bottleneck Isn't Technology

I'm 50 years old, I've seen too many technology waves.

Every time a wave comes, everyone discusses "can the technology do it." But what finally determines the outcome is never the technology itself, but "what humans want."

The internet can connect everyone, but what did we use it for? Watching short videos, reading gossip, arguing with each other.

AI can help humans solve many problems, but the prerequisite is—we first need to think clearly, what problems do we actually want to solve.

Schulman says "defining goals will be humanity's last bastion," the subtext of this sentence is: in terms of technical capability, we might not be able to hold on; but on the matter of "what we want," we must hold on.

Middle-aged people's biggest advantage isn't learning things quickly, but having seen enough cycles to know what's important and what's not.

V. In Conclusion

AI surpassing top experts in 3-4 years, whether this prediction is accurate, I don't know.

But I know one thing: panic is useless, seeing clearly is useful.

See clearly what AI can do, use it as a tool. See clearly what AI can't do, hold onto your judgment. See clearly what you want to do, don't be pushed by anxiety.

3-4 years, not long, not short. Enough for you to see the direction clearly, and enough for you to prepare.

No need to panic, but stay clear-headed. Middle-aged people's core competitiveness has never been speed, it's judgment.

At the recently concluded Code with Claude 2026 conference, Anthropic released a feature I've read through three times: Dreaming—letting AI learn to "dream."

You read that right, dreaming.

This isn't a gimmick. Anthropic added a background process to Claude's agent platform, letting AI automatically enter a "sleep" state between tasks, reviewing past conversation records, organizing memory banks, discovering recurring error patterns, then generating optimized new memories.

In 50-year-old terms: isn't this just what the human brain does at night when sleeping? Integrating fragmented knowledge learned during the day into long-term memory.

"We're no longer just making chatbots, we're making self-evolving collaborators."

— Dario Amodei

I. Three Core Capabilities, One Logic

First, Dreaming (dream memory distillation). Runs periodically in the background, reads up to the last 100 historical conversations, merging duplicate data, updating outdated entries, distilling macro patterns. After legal tech company Harvey used it, task completion rates increased about 6 times.

Second, Outcomes (result-driven execution). Developers define "success criteria," the system assigns independent scoring agents to grade AI, if it doesn't meet standards it's sent back for rewriting. Internal tests show docx document generation success rate improved 8.4%, pptx improved 10.1%.

Third, Multiagent Orchestration. The main agent breaks tasks into multiple subtasks, assigning them to specialized sub-agents for parallel processing. In a lunar mining drone landing simulation, safety scores went from 67% to 100%.

The underlying logic of these three capabilities is just one: letting AI go from "starting from zero each time" to "cross-session cumulative learning."

"This isn't a tool upgrade, this is AI's role qualitatively changing from screwdriver to employee."

II. The Hidden Battle Over Computing Power

You might have noticed, the hottest news from this conference was actually Anthropic signing an agreement with SpaceX—renting all computing power from Musk's Colossus 1 data center, including 220,000 Nvidia GPUs.

This is interesting. Three months ago Musk was publicly calling Anthropic "anti-human and evil," now he's renting all computing power to them.

But what I see isn't just business cooperation, it's a deeper signal: computing power is becoming AI companies' biggest strategic bottleneck. Anthropic's first quarter revenue exploded 80 times, expectations were only 10 times, the result is they simply can't handle it.

Moreover, Musk hid a clause in the agreement: if Anthropic's AI does something harmful to humans, SpaceX has the right to take back computing power at any time. What's this called? A "self-destruct switch." Renting it to you, but can pull your plug at any time.

III. What Should Domestic Companies Benchmark Against?

Domestic Manus, ByteDance Coze, Alibaba's agent platforms are all catching up to this "Agents as Infrastructure" narrative line, letting enterprises build AI agents with zero code. But Anthropic has already run to the next stage—letting agents "cross-session self-evolve."

This is no longer competition over "how to make tools useful," but competition over "AI employee maturity."

IV. A Fifty-Year-Old Perspective

I'm 50 years old this year, I've experienced the entire cycle of the internet from nothing to something. Looking back at the past twenty years, technology revolutions are often not triggered by any single product, but by a certain "paradigm shift."

From command line to graphical interface was a paradigm shift. From desktop to mobile was a paradigm shift.

AI going from "Q&A tool" to "self-evolving collaborator" might be the next paradigm shift.

Dreaming's significance isn't in the gimmick of "AI can dream," but in: Anthropic is seriously thinking about one problem—how to let AI get better and better without humans watching.

For enterprises, this means AI employee training costs will get lower and lower, adaptation speed will get faster and faster. You teach it once today, tomorrow it might be able to summarize patterns on its own.

Of course, we're still far from true "autonomous evolution." Dreaming is currently still in research preview stage. But the trend is already very clear—AI is moving from being used to being a collaborator.

As entrepreneurs, the question we should ask isn't "will AI replace humans," but "how do I make AI my smartest employee."

"Future enterprise competitiveness isn't about how many AI tools you have, but to what extent you let AI evolve."

— BanbaiGuan AI

💡 Action Suggestions

If you're an enterprise manager:

  • Evaluate whether existing AI tools support "cross-session memory"—if not, it's starting from zero each time
  • Focus on multi-agent orchestration implementation scenarios—which business processes can be broken into subtasks for parallel processing
  • Establish AI output scoring standards—like Outcomes, use rules not feelings to evaluate AI quality

If you're an AI practitioner:

  • Research Dreaming's technical implementation approach: asynchronous memory organization + human review + incremental optimization
  • Think about how to migrate this approach to domestic large model application layers

# Stop Blindly Lengthening Your Prompts! The True Logic of Using AI Efficiently Is Backwards for 90% of People

After playing around with AI for over half a year, I've summarized a highly counterintuitive truth:

**Dumping all your pre-thought-out requirements at once and asking AI a question is actually the least efficient way to use it.**

Many have already avoided the beginner's trap of just typing in a single-sentence prompt.

Sitting in front of the computer and opening the AI chat window, we carefully organize our words, writing out a long, seemingly detailed set of requirements:

> Help me write a marketing campaign plan targeting SME clients. The style should be pragmatic, with a word count of around 3,000 words. The structure should include background, objectives, execution steps, and budget.

It looks like the information provided is sufficiently comprehensive and well-organized, and we consider the requirements fully communicated.

But after extensive hands-on practice, you'll discover a common dilemma:

**Even if you write a lengthy prompt, the final output from the AI is still rarely ready for direct implementation.**

## I. Our Biggest Misconception: Assuming "Write Whatever Comes to Mind" = Complete Requirements

When I first started using AI, my mindset was the same as the vast majority of people:

As long as I write down every possible requirement I can think of, the AI can deliver content that is ready to use right away.

It wasn't until I tried it dozens of times that I gradually realized something:

**AI cannot read your mind and decipher the unspoken information hidden in your head.**

You possess industry experience, project background, implicit constraints, and expected standards. These things have long existed in your cognition, so you subconsciously assume the AI should naturally know them.

But if you don't proactively write them into the prompt, the AI can only rely on generic templates to respond.

The final output may seem to have a complete framework, but in reality, it deviates from your actual scenarios at every turn. The key points remain superficial, merely scratching the surface.

What follows is endless revisions, supplementary instructions, and regenerations, resulting in a tedious back-and-forth tug-of-war.

You originally wanted to use AI to save time, but in the end, you end up expending a massive amount of energy on continuous tweaking.

## II. A Complete Reversal of Thinking: Stop Chasing the AI with Questions; Let the AI Ask You First

The huge gap between people in using AI doesn't lie in how many obscure prompt spells they've mastered, but rather in a completely different workflow.

**Average User Mode**: Organize the requirements you can think of → Send them to the AI all at once → Wait for the results → Discover flaws and revise repeatedly

**Efficient Mode**: Set up rules to have the AI proactively ask questions → Fully excavate all explicit + implicit requirements → After consolidating the information, generate the final content

Here is a prompt I've refined through numerous projects that you can copy and paste directly:

> From now on, act as my dedicated collaboration consultant. Before I explicitly provide the final task requirements, you must not start generating any content directly. First, regarding the task I am about to undertake, ask me 10 consecutive, most critical clarifying questions across the following dimensions: objectives, applicable scenarios, delivery format, detail requirements, and relevant background information I already have. Once I have answered all these questions, compile a complete and clear requirements list based on all the information I've provided, and only then begin generating the corresponding final content.

💡 Two core rules, highly recommended to be highlighted:

**① Prohibit the AI from outputting content without prior communication, eliminating templated, ineffective text**

**② Through 10 targeted questions, force ourselves to sort out the implicit conditions overlooked in our minds**

Many times, it's not that the AI isn't intelligent enough; it's that we ourselves cannot sort out all the requirements clearly in one go. Leveraging the AI's reverse questioning is like having a dedicated consultant helping us identify and fill in the gaps.

## III. Real Project Testing: Thorough Requirements Sorting Cuts Rework Time in Half

I have continuously compared the difference between the two usage methods across multiple projects, and the results are highly intuitive.

**Previously**: Even if I wrote a very long prompt, I would still miss key boundary conditions. The AI output often required five or six rounds of revisions—adjusting details, supplementing background, and correcting direction—before it barely met the standards for implementation.

**Now**: Paste the above instruction, and the AI will continuously ask targeted questions about the task.

After I answer them one by one, all vague ideas are concretized. The final generated content aligns highly with expectations, often taking perfect shape on the first try without the need for repeated adjustments.

**Conservatively estimated, this method saves me at least half the time spent on AI debugging, bidding farewell to endless, ineffective trial and error.**

## IV. No Need to Be Obsessed with a Massive Amount of Tutorials; Grasping the Core Logic Trumps Everything

Online, you can easily find prompt tutorials that are hundreds of pages long and all sorts of AI usage tips. Many people frantically bookmark them and study everywhere.

But most people still find it hard to put what they've learned into practice, which is essentially putting the cart before the horse.

People are overly fixated on sentence structures, wording, and various advanced instructions, while ignoring the most fundamental level: **The upper limit of AI output quality depends on the completeness of the requirements.**

Flashy techniques can be accumulated gradually, but this mindset of "clarify requirements first, then generate content" can be implemented immediately.

Solidly mastering this single prompt is far more practical than learning dozens of fragmented tricks.

## Final Thoughts

AI is not a black box that generates finished products with a single click.

Don't just compete to see who can write longer prompts. Learning to build a process and excavating all the implicit requirements hidden in your mind is the core of using AI well.

Starting now, try to change your usage habits: stop dumping all your thoughts at once, and learn to let the AI proactively ask you questions.

In 2026, 78% of enterprises are already using AI in at least one business process.

Writing code, creating designs, generating proposals, analyzing data—AI can do it all, and it does it just as well as humans. The technical barrier has shifted from "three years of study" to "knowing how to ask the right questions."

But here's the question: do you know how to ask?

The scarcest resource in the AI era isn't people who know how to operate tools, but those who know what problems the tools should solve.

▎I. After the Democratization of Technology, the Humanities Are the Moat

The global AI market is valued at $391 billion, with corporate AI spending surging toward $1.5 trillion.

Yet, after surveying 65 senior data scientists and engineers, the RAND Corporation uncovered a sobering statistic: over 80% of AI projects fail.

That's twice the failure rate of non-AI IT projects.

Money is burning, technology is iterating, but projects are stalling.

Why? The technology isn't the problem. The problem is that no one knows what problems the technology should actually solve.

I learned this the hard way when developing an AIoT smart shelf system.

The tech team spent two months pushing shelf recognition accuracy from 98.5% to 99.9%, and everyone was thrilled during the presentation.

Then the client took a look and said:

"Your technology is indeed impressive, but what I need isn't to know when a single screw is missing from the warehouse. What I need is for customers to keep coming back to me for their orders."

That statement was a wake-up call.

Technology solves "how to count accurately," but the reason customers pay is always "how to make me more money."

Technology determines how fast you can go, but the humanities determine which direction you should take.

▎II. How the "Uselessness of Liberal Arts" Myth Fooled You

Over the past decade, "master math, physics, and chemistry" has been treated as the only correct answer.

Parents urge their children to choose computer science, finance, or engineering, discouraging the humanities with a single excuse: "It's hard to find a job."

But this judgment is built on two premises.

First, the technical barrier is high, out of reach for liberal arts students.

Second, AI won't replace basic technical jobs.

Now, both premises have collapsed simultaneously.

AI has shaved the technical barrier from a sheer cliff into a gentle staircase.

Knowing how to write Python is no longer a rare skill, because AI writes it faster, more accurately, and without bugs.

Those who used to rely on technical barriers to make a living suddenly find their biggest advantage reduced to "I can also do it with AI."

Meanwhile, the very skills liberal arts students have been honing—understanding human nature, constructing narratives, evaluating value, and making cross-disciplinary connections—are precisely the ones AI finds hardest to replicate.

AI can write a grammatically flawless essay, but it cannot write the sentence that truly leaves people speechless.

Because silence isn't a grammar issue; it's an empathy issue.

I'm not saying STEM students aren't capable.

I'm saying that over the past decade, our definition of "useful" has been far too narrow.

So narrow that we only look at whether one can write code or calculate models, while ignoring a more crucial ability: knowing what to calculate and who to calculate it for.

You might think the humanities are exiting the stage, but in reality, STEM is being forced to catch up on its missed lessons.

Reading this, you might be wondering: as a liberal arts student, what should I be doing now? The following section holds the answer.

▎III. AI Isn't Here to Work for Liberal Arts Students; It's Here to Amplify Their Capabilities

78% of enterprises are using AI, yet 80% of AI projects are failing.

The gap isn't technical ability; it's business understanding and communicative judgment.

And this is precisely the domain where liberal arts students excel.

Communication majors know how to make information resonate with people.

Psychology majors know why users hesitate.

Sociology majors know how to drive organizational change.

History majors know which models have succeeded in the past and which have died out.

AI is a super megaphone.

But what it amplifies isn't technology; it's the user's judgment.

For those with good judgment, AI can amplify their impact tenfold or a hundredfold.

For those with poor judgment, using AI just means generating garbage faster.

I verified this logic myself when working in new media operations.

Using AI to assist with copywriting indeed boosted efficiency by three to four times.

But the decisive elements—topic direction, emotional anchors, reader resonance—still rely entirely on human perception and judgment.

AI helped me take a 60-point idea up to 85 points.

But it won't help me find that 60-point starting point.

Where that starting point lies depends on how much of the world you have seen.

AI isn't responsible for helping you find your direction; it's only responsible for taking your direction much further.

▎IV. The Lesson Liberal Arts Students Need Isn't Technology, It's "Translational Ability"

Saying "it's time for liberal arts students to step up" doesn't mean you can sit back and wait for the market to fight over you without learning anything new.

You need to make up for one subject: Translational Ability.

What is translational ability? It's translating your professional judgment into a language AI can understand, into a proposal your boss can comprehend, and into value that customers are willing to pay for.

Here are three concrete actions.

Step one: Learn to use AI as an assistant, not a crutch.

Don't expect AI to make judgments for you; instead, let it help you validate your judgments and accelerate execution.

Spend 30 minutes every day testing the capability boundaries of AI tools in different scenarios. A smartphone and a browser are all you need. The barrier to entry is ridiculously low, yet the return is ten times higher than learning to code.

Step two: Build your "Humanities + X" cross-disciplinary advantage.

Literature majors should learn a bit about data, history majors about product, and psychology majors about business.

The intersection is the blue ocean.

Those in a single discipline are fiercely competing in their own little wells, while cross-disciplinary individuals are already building bridges between them.

Step three: Have the courage to tell the tech team, "This direction is wrong."

Not because you understand technology better than they do, but because you understand people better than they do.

And this ability is highly valued in the AI era.

The weapon for liberal arts students isn't to fight AI, but to command it.

▎V. Why I Believe This Judgment

I've taken my fair share of tumbles across several industries.

In finance, I've seen the most meticulously calculated models fail to withstand human panic.

In retail, I've seen the best products pile up in warehouses simply because they couldn't tell a good story.

In AIoT, I've seen the most technologically advanced solutions turned away at the door with a single phrase: "You don't understand our industry."

Every single time, the ultimate winner wasn't the one with the strongest technology.

It was the one that understood people the best.

This isn't just feel-good rhetoric I've made up.

This is a path I've paved step by step, in supply chains, at client sites, and through countless nights of "the technical solution is perfect but it just won't sell."

The speed of technological iteration has already surpassed the limits of human learning capacity.

You can't maintain your competitiveness simply by "learning more technology," because there will always be people and AI who learn faster than you.

But you can maintain your irreplaceability by "understanding people better."

Because AI won't live your life for you.

Only humans can truly understand humans.

AI is not the opponent of liberal arts students; it is the megaphone they have been waiting for.

The flatter the technical barrier, the deeper the moat of the humanities.

This isn't some optimistic prediction; it is a reality that has already happened and is now accelerating.

Those who were told from childhood that "the humanities are useless" have finally reached their moment of comeback.

The more AI rages, the more valuable the humanities become. This isn't a slogan; it's a calculable reality.

What do you think is the biggest advantage for liberal arts students in the AI era? Let's chat in the comments.

If you found this useful, share it with those around you who have been troubled by the "uselessness of the humanities" myth.

In business, some people spend every day networking over drinks and running from one social circle to another, growing more exhausted by the day; while others can close deals with just a laptop, skipping dinner parties and socializing entirely, yet still holding tens of millions in assets.

The demographic dividend of personal connections that the older generation relied on is fading. What now supports ordinary people in building long-term wealth is their own unique core competency.

01 An Extremely Polarized Market: It’s Not That There’s No Money, It’s That the Money Has Changed Hands

If you observe the current market closely, you will notice an extremely polarized yet undeniably real phenomenon.

Moutai, once hailed as the "hard currency" of the business world, has seen its annual performance decline for the first time in over two decades since going public. Porsche, a long-time symbol of high-end prestige, has seen its domestic sales drop for four consecutive years, plunging 26% last year alone.

Yet on the other side of the market, things are booming beyond imagination.

In Shenzhen, a 50-million-yuan oceanview luxury penthouse sold out just half an hour after its launch. Even more thought-provoking is that nearly 40% of today's buyers for tens-of-millions-yuan luxury homes are post-90s.

These young people are mostly deeply engaged in AI, chips, new energy, and hard tech. Relying neither on connections to pave the way nor on social circles for endorsement, many have leveraged their own strength to buy high-end properties in full cash, steadily capturing the dividends of the era.

This is the most brutal and authentic shift of our times: wealth has never disappeared; it has simply adopted a completely new settlement method.

In the past, wealth was secured by leveraging connections and resources; now, it is realized through hard-core core competencies. The old logic of making money through personal favors is gradually failing, while a brand-new logic of value creation is taking full control of the market.

02 The Old Money Era: The Means of Production Were Connections; The Nouveau Riche Era: The Means of Production Are Three Things

Looking back over the past few decades, when the older generation did business and accumulated wealth, they never competed on product advantages or technological barriers.

In that era, information was closed off, industry resources were scarce, and market channels were monopolized. Land, licenses, orders, and channels were all limited resources. Whoever had the toughest circle, the broadest network, and the best skills in socializing to maintain relationships could secure resources, reap the dividends, and make money steadily.

Resources don't just tilt in your favor for no reason; the core relies on "trust." And the business trust of the older generation was never proven by sheer capability, but was built bit by bit through endless banquets, displays of grandeur, and exchanges of personal favors.

Such traditional bosses are ubiquitous and highly representative around us.

Daily dinners costing thousands of yuan and bottles of Moutai worth tens of thousands might seem extravagantly wasteful and vain to outsiders. But those who understand business know that this is never mere consumption; it is a rigid investment in doing business, a core bargaining chip for exchanging resources and maintaining trust.

Luxury mansions are social facades, but also bank collateral; luxury cars are means of transport, but also endorsements of strength; Moutai is a beverage, but also the hard currency circulating in the realm of social obligations.

In the days of imperfect rules and opaque information, this logic was perfectly sound. Without relying on personal favors or grand displays, ordinary people could never access premium resources, let alone seize business opportunities.

But looking at it today, the core means of production for the two groups have completely diverged.

The means of production that old money relies on are connections and relationships; while the truly valuable means of production in the hands of the nouveau riche come down to just three things: cognition, time, and health.

One person with one laptop can independently create value. This explains why these tech entrepreneurs barely need to socialize frequently, skip drinking parties, and avoid banquets. It’s not that they consider themselves aloof; it’s simply completely unnecessary.

Their deals are closed on the product and data fronts. They don't need to build relationships over drinks, nor do they need to visit people and ask for favors. The demand for interpersonal connections has plummeted, and naturally, the value of goods that circulate through social relationships, like Moutai, has shrunk significantly.

The decline in Moutai is never about the price of the liquor itself, but rather the pricing of the "relationship" asset. Since people no longer need to maintain resources through dinner parties, the social attributes of baijiu naturally drop to zero—this is the market's most straightforward answer. In fact, a massive number of micro-enterprises founded by solo entrepreneurs never need to cultivate complex networks from start to finish.

Once you understand the difference in the means of production, comparing the consumption choices of the two generations makes all these phenomena easily explainable.

Take luxury mansions, for example. Old money buys big houses as a facade to show off to the outside world; the nouveau riche buy tens-of-millions-yuan properties as tools to enhance efficiency, with core demands being living comfort and saving commute time. The young people in Shenzhen buying 50-million-yuan mansions treat a short commute as an absolute necessity. They buy homes for their own quality of life, not to put on a show for others.

The logic for cars is exactly the same: the older generation buys cars focused on the logo to show off their strength to clients; the nouveau riche value intelligent driving more, seeking hassle-free and comfortable rides. Tesla's full self-driving capability, which frees up their time, is far more attractive than any car badge.

The contrast in watches is even more intuitive. The watches of traditional tycoons are "status meters" used to display their identity to the outside world; the nouveau riche wear smartwatches, focusing only on heart rate and sleep monitoring, serving as a dashboard to manage their own physical condition.

The latest Hurun Report also confirms this shift: on the business gifting list, traditional watches have dropped from first to fourth place, while digital electronic products have shot straight to the top.

Underlying these consumption choices is a shift in how people perceive the "body."

The older generation was accustomed to trading health for connections and orders; every drink was essentially overdrawn against their body in exchange for trust. The new generation of entrepreneurs is the exact opposite: they reject ineffective drinking parties, preferring to hike, run, and work out. They proactively spend money on maintaining their health and getting regular physicals. To them, the body is the core means of production for creating value.

The root cause of Arc'teryx's 50% year-over-year revenue surge in China lies right here. When the body is the core asset, outdoor, sports, and health consumption naturally continue to explode. Old money makes money at the banquet table; the nouveau riche create value at their desks and computers. Capital naturally flows into tracks that elevate the self and nurture the mind and body.

It is also important to state objectively here that this is not to deny the older generation's way of survival.

Industry veterans have previously discussed that we shouldn't blindly belittle the generation that did business through personal favors. In an environment characterized by vague property rights, opaque information, and an imperfect social credit system, demonstrating one's credit through high-end consumption was the most pragmatic and efficient survival strategy. It wasn't that they chose extravagant socializing; it was that the business rules of that era could only be priced this way.

The shift in the rules of the times doesn't mean there is a hierarchy between the two groups. But we must also see objectively: the nouveau riche have their own "Moutai" as well. High-end outdoor gear, limited-edition digital products, and smart mobility devices may seem like self-improvement, but essentially, they are also a brand-new set of identity-paying symbols.

The desire to show off and divide into social circles is an unchanging human nature. The only difference is that the language of display has changed: in the past, it was performed for resource holders; now, it is used to screen for like-minded peers. Human nature has never changed; only the symbols identifying identity have undergone iteration.

03 The New Money Era: Making Money Shifts from "Seeking Outward" to "Rooting Inward"

The times have completely changed. Today's rapidly rising young entrepreneurs and tech nouveau riche have a way of making money that runs completely counter to the older generation.

Old money makes money by always seeking outward: asking others for favors, building connections, mingling in social circles, and relying on others to dispense opportunities and allocate resources.

The nouveau riche make money by always rooting inward: deeply cultivating technology, refining products, and accumulating value. Relying on their own hard-core capabilities, they realize results in the market and create wealth.

Take Changxin Memory Technologies (688825.SH), the Hefei-based memory chip company that went public yesterday, for example. After the listing, all of its more than 6,000 employees hold shares. Ordinary employees easily achieve a net worth of millions, while core backbone members boast net worths in the tens of millions.

Their wealth wasn't achieved through personal favors or connections. It was the solid value return earned by the team grinding away at technology and deeply cultivating the sector for a decade, ultimately being recognized by the market and capital.

Precisely because of this, they have absolutely no need for luxury cars, mansions, or famous watches to gild their image or create momentum. The technology in their hands, the landed products, the equity they hold, and their accumulated professional track record are the most hard-core and reliable identity cards.

04 A Complete Reversal in Consumption Values: From "Pleasing Others" to "Investing in Oneself"

The iteration of the logic of making money has also completely rewritten the public's consumption and values.

When the older generation buys houses, cars, or luxury goods, it is essentially "buying to show others," in order to save face, stabilize their social circles, and secure business. Meanwhile, for the new generation of entrepreneurs, all consumption prioritizes pleasing themselves. They value living comfort when buying homes, hassle-free efficiency when buying cars, and focus on maintaining energy and caring for health in daily consumption.

Businesspeople in the past were accustomed to trading health for connections and wealth; the new entrepreneurs today consistently adhere to making money to sustain themselves, using their income to maintain energy, accumulate cognition, and invest in themselves.

This is also the core reason for the sustained strong sales of smart devices, health equipment, and high-end outdoor gear. Arc'teryx's 50% year-over-year revenue surge in China is not essentially about following trends, but rather because smart people have realized a truth: the most valuable means of production in the new era are the human body, energy, and cognition, rather than solidified interpersonal connections.

05 The Era Hasn't Eliminated People, Only Outdated Logic

Some might ask, is the new business model necessarily more advanced than the old one?

Not exactly. Human nature has never changed; what has changed is only the survival gameplay of the times.

In the past, business circles were divided by Moutai, luxury cars, and mansions; today, like-minded partners are screened by cognition, professionalism, and capability. At the end of the day, it's all about circle screening. The only difference is: in the past, it was about pleasing resource holders; now, it's about matching with fellow travelers.

The rise and fall of market prices represent the entire society voting with real money. To see the shift of wealth and power, you don't need to stare at the rich lists; understanding the rise and fall of prices is enough to see the trend.

Moutai sales are declining while outdoor tech categories are rising; traditional real estate appreciation is slowing down while chip and hard tech continue to soar. The market has already provided the answer.

Many seniors around us who are deeply engaged in traditional industries were the winners of the last era. They caught the dividends of connections and real estate, accumulating massive wealth, yet they struggle to adapt to the new era's rules. In their youth, they were busy with socializing and hustling, neglecting their health and alienating their families. In their twilight years, they live alone in empty houses, their lives a mess of trivialities. Looking back at their experiences, one can't help but sigh: if they had known to care for their health and nurture their families in their youth, it would have been a completely different life.

The era of the personal connection dividend has come to an end, but cherishing your health, treating your family well, and working diligently are eternal truths, no matter the era.

What truly deserves our clear understanding is the unchanging underlying competitive logic of the times.

In the past, doing business only required being down-to-earth, hardworking, honest, and having reliable products. Add a bit of worldly wisdom and a decent network, and you could establish a firm foothold and make money continuously.

But now, this logic is long outdated. Relying solely on hard work, integrity, and traditional products is simply not enough to gain a foothold in the market.

Today's market has long since completely bid farewell to the era of personal connection dividends and fully entered the era of value competition.

Today's business competition doesn't rely on connections, dividends, or face. It competes on technological barriers, cognitive gaps, and core competitiveness that others cannot copy or replace. Without exclusive hard-core capabilities, one is destined to be slowly eliminated by the market.

Final Thoughts

The logic of making money has long been quietly rewritten:

In the past, making money relied on the dividends of the times, personal connections and resources, and keeping one's head down and working hard;

In the future, making money will no longer compete on the breadth of connections or the face of social circles, but on just one thing—whether you possess core value that others cannot replicate.

The old era of making a living through personal favors and saving face has completely ebbed away.

The new era of establishing oneself through capability, value, and hard-core strength is just rising.

In this era of rapid iteration, connections may bring temporary opportunities, but one's own core capability is the wealth that accompanies you for life and never depreciates.

The wealth-preservation mindset of smart people is always to root inward, investing energy and capital into themselves and their families. Those who blindly rely on external circles and facades to put on a show will easily lose everything once the wind of the times changes direction.

May we all break free from the limitations of connection-based thinking, deeply cultivate ourselves, and accumulate value, rooting ourselves firmly and moving forward steadily on the new track of the times.

You've always felt like you haven't taken action—

But what if it's your definition of "action" that's wrong?

Is "difficulty taking action" really about laziness, or is it just that the threshold for "action" in your mind is set way too high?

You feel like you should study AI for two hours every day, but you never even get started. But if you change your goal to "open an AI chat tool and ask one question a day," you might achieve it in the very first week.

The problem isn't that you don't take action—it's that your very definition of "action" excludes you from the start.

Take an American named Stephen Guise. Back in 2012, he was out of shape and living a sluggish life. Like everyone else, he set a New Year's resolution every year: "Exercise for thirty minutes every day." And like everyone else, he never made it past the second week.

Then he made a decision that barely felt like a decision. He changed "exercise for thirty minutes every day" to "do just one push-up every day." One. Just one. No pressure to do any more.

His reasoning was that a single push-up is so simple that anyone can do it at any time, leaving the brain with no excuse to resist. The result? Once he got down on the floor, he figured, "Well, I'm already down here, I might as well do a few more." That day, he exercised for thirty minutes. He later wrote a book about this method called Mini Habits, which became a global bestseller.

What Guise actually did was just one thing: he redefined what "exercise" means. Originally, in his brain, "exercise" meant thirty minutes of cardio. Under that definition, the daily situation was always, "The conditions aren't right today, I'll do it tomorrow." But once he redefined "exercise" as "doing one push-up"—the conditions were met every single day. Every single day was a successful day.

Psychologists discovered a principle as early as 1908, known as the Yerkes-Dodson Law. Its conclusion runs completely counter to our intuition: for difficult tasks, the stronger your motivation and the greater your resolve, the lower your efficiency actually becomes. They mapped this out as an inverted U-shaped curve—if motivation is too weak, you won't move, which is easy to understand. But if motivation is too strong, you won't move either. Because when your brain receives an instruction like "exercise for thirty minutes every day" or "study AI for two hours every day," it automatically triggers an evaluation process: Do I have enough time? Enough energy? What if I can't pull it off? The evaluation concludes "high cost, high risk," and the brain switches to avoidance mode. So you pick up your phone and scroll through short videos for forty minutes.

It's not that you're lazy. It's that your definition of "action" has already scared your brain into retreating before you've even done anything.

Meanwhile, "doing one push-up" is judged by the brain as zero cost and zero risk. Cleared for takeoff. Once you're down on the floor, your body's momentum takes over. What Guise changed wasn't the standard; it was the definition itself.

This principle applies to learning AI even more directly than you might think.

Inside the Huawei HarmonyOS phone you're using right now, there's a built-in AI assistant named Xiaoyi. You might have used it to set alarms or check the weather, but its capabilities go far beyond that. Today, we'll just focus on one feature called "Xiaoyi Tasks." This isn't traditional voice command stuff where you say something and it does one thing. Xiaoyi Tasks is an AI-driven automation system. Its logic boils down to this: you tell it a rule in plain language, the AI understands your intent on its own, automatically generates a task, and then executes it for you when the conditions are met.

For example, you say to your phone right now: "Every day at 8 AM, read out today's schedule."

That's it. Just that one sentence. The AI parses "every day at 8 AM" as the trigger condition and "read out the schedule" as the action. Starting tomorrow morning, the moment you open your eyes, your phone will automatically read out all your meetings, to-dos, and reminders for the day. You don't need to unlock your phone, find the calendar app, tap into it to check, or even remember to do it. You say it once, and the AI runs it automatically every day from then on.

This is exactly like Guise doing his push-ups. In your previous definition, "learning AI" meant "studying it systematically for two hours every day." That definition alone kept you out the door. But if you redefine it as "opening your phone and saying one sentence to it"—the barrier disappears. You've crossed it.

Let's go one level deeper. You want to connect to WiFi when you get home and turn it off when you leave to save battery. Doing it manually every day is a hassle, but not worth the trouble of setting up properly. You just say: "Automatically turn on WiFi when I get home, and automatically turn it off when I leave." The AI understands "getting home" as the location condition and "turning on WiFi" as the action, automatically generating a rule. From then on, this task completely disappears from your daily life.

Let's go one level deeper still. Your mom waits for you to top up her phone credit every month. Sometimes you're busy and forget, and at the end of the month she calls to remind you, leaving you feeling both guilty and annoyed. You just say: "Top up 100 yuan for my mom's phone at 10 AM on the 1st of every month." The AI automatically parses the time, recipient, action, and amount, executing it on time every month. You will never forget again.

You need to head out at 8 AM tomorrow, but the weather is uncertain. You don't have to get up, check the weather, decide whether to call a cab, and then open the ride-hailing app—that chain of decisions has to happen in the mere twenty minutes between waking up and leaving, which is already tight. The night before, you just say: "At 8 AM tomorrow, if it's raining, book a cab to the office for me." The AI checks the weather automatically at that time and books the ride for you.

It's not that you can't learn these things, or that you're getting older and your memory is failing, or that there's a gap between you and new technology. It's simply that you never knew the AI in your phone could already be used this way. Once you know, and you try it just once, it becomes second nature to you. And the starting point of that instinct is just you redefining one thing—what it means to "start using AI."

Change "learning AI" from "studying for two hours every day" to "saying one sentence to your phone." This time, instead of receiving an avoidance signal of "this is too hard, forget it," your brain gets positive feedback: "I did it." This positive feedback is the only fuel that will keep you going.

There's so much more Xiaoyi Tasks can do—flash alerts for incoming calls, voice announcements when charging is complete, automatically locking screen rotation when opening the camera, and restoring rotation when exiting a video app. How many things in your life require you to remember them and do them manually every single time? You probably haven't thought seriously about it, because you assume "that's just how it is." But it shouldn't be.

I'll write a dedicated, comprehensive tutorial and break it all down for you from start to finish.

But before that, do just one thing first. Right now, pick up your Huawei phone and say your first sentence to it.

The World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC), which takes the internet by storm every year, is exceptionally different this year.

In previous years, WAIC-related content on our feeds was all about cool, cutting-edge tech: dancing robots, AI writing poetry, and smart special effects pushed to the max.

It looked astonishing and avant-garde, but most people just sighed after watching: "Technology is truly amazing, but it has absolutely nothing to do with my ordinary life."

But the 2026 WAIC has completely changed the game.

After going through all the hot exhibits, industry trends, and keynotes by industry leaders at the conference, I discovered the most striking and authentic trend:

AI has completely shed its gimmicks and hype. It's no longer about empty promises, storytelling, or showing off concepts. Instead, it is fully dedicated to practical implementation, creating value, and making real money.

This year's AI conference features no out-of-reach future tech; it's all about real changes that closely relate to ordinary people's work, life, making money, and saving money.

Today, without obscure industry jargon or overly complex industry analysis, I'll use plain language that everyone can understand to break down exactly what changes closely related to each and every one of us are hidden in the 2026 WAIC that has taken the internet by storm.

01 Robots No Longer Perform Tricks; They're Here to Take Over Ordinary People's Hard Physical Labor

In the exhibitions over the past two years, robots mainly focused on "looks and talent."

They were uniformly humanoid, capable of boxing, dancing, and doing backflips, more like performers on a stage designed to catch the eye and show off technology.

But all the robots revealed at this year's WAIC have collectively "landed jobs," completely bidding farewell to flashy stunts.

People are no longer obsessed with a uniform humanoid appearance; how good-looking they are doesn't matter at all. The only criteria are whether they can do the job, their efficiency, and low cost.

In flat factories, warehouses, and supermarkets, wheeled robots are everywhere, handling, sorting, and patrolling 24/7 without needing rest, paychecks, or management. They are steadily replacing ordinary workers in repetitive, tedious, and basic manual labor.

In dangerous and complex scenarios like mountain roads, construction sites, and emergency rescue, heavy-duty quadruped robots have become the main force. With a 300-kilogram body, they can carry a ton of supplies and work continuously for seven or eight hours. They can navigate the rough and dangerous roads that ordinary people can't walk on, taking on all high-risk and heavy physical tasks.

Most importantly, these are not just prototypes for display; they have all been commercially deployed and are working in batches. They have long been quietly popularized in logistics warehouses, pharmacies, and factory assembly lines.

We have to admit: in the future, jobs that rely purely on physical strength, are repetitive, and highly intensive will only become fewer and fewer.

02 The Most Realistic Truth for Adults: Hard Things Don't Necessarily Make Money, but Essential Needs Do

Many people have always had a misconception: the harder the task and the more high-end the technology, the easier it is to make money.

But the numerous projects revealed at this year's WAIC have completely overturned this ingrained perception.

A clothes-folding robot went viral at the exhibition, pushing technical difficulty to the max. Home environments are messy, clothes have wrinkles and different materials, plus interference from lighting and clutter. For the robot to accurately identify and neatly fold clothes is extremely difficult. Enterprises have trained on hundreds of millions of data points and invested huge R&D costs for this.

Yet, despite being such a high-difficulty product, it has almost no market and no one is willing to pay for it.

The reason is simple: folding clothes is technically very hard, but its commercial value is very low.

It's not a rigid demand; not folding today or organizing tomorrow won't affect life at all. Ordinary people would rather spend a few dozen bucks to hire a cleaner to get it done than pay for expensive smart equipment.

In contrast, seemingly ordinary industrial robots that screw bolts, plug in wire harnesses, and sort parts have a technical difficulty far lower than the clothes-folding robot, yet they are making a killing.

Because these tasks are directly related to the factory's production capacity, efficiency, and cost. Every extra minute the machine works, the enterprise can make more money and lose less. It's a solid, rigid commercial demand.

Applied to us ordinary people, the logic is equally clear:

Your income never depends on how hard the things you do are, but on whether what you do can solve others' rigid demands and help them save or make money.

03 AI Giants Are Fiercely Competing; Ordinary People's New Money-Making Opportunities Lie in the Supporting Tracks

Many people get more anxious the more they watch: with AI getting stronger and robots becoming more widespread, are ordinary people completely out of opportunities?

Actually, it's the exact opposite. This WAIC has released a signal that ordinary people should grasp most: while giants compete fiercely in high-end complete machines, ordinary people should compete in segmented supporting fields. Huge amounts of steady, small-profit businesses are hidden in these niche tracks.

Nowadays, there are more and more giants building robots and large models. The main track is severely hyper-competitive, and profit margins are getting thinner. But the supporting industries serving AI and robots are quietly making a fortune.

Some people specialize in building virtual training grounds for robots. No need for real venues or physical trial and error; they simulate various complex scenarios in virtual space, allowing robots to repeatedly practice obstacle avoidance, grasping, and movement. Almost all robot enterprises need this service, steadily reaping the dividends of the entire industry.

Some delve deep into affordable robot components. Traditional robotic arms cost tens of thousands of yuan per set, with an extremely high entry barrier. The new bionic tendon robotic arm replicates the human body structure and greatly compresses costs. It can be deployed for just 8,000 yuan and can stably grasp millions of times, perfectly matching the needs of logistics, small factories, and small shops, achieving high-volume sales and continuous profitability.

The biggest dividend in the AI era has never been for everyone to build high-end AI or chase the trends.

Giants are responsible for creating the trends, while ordinary people do the supporting work, provide services, and handle implementation—they can still steadily get their share of the era's dividends.

04 Big Data Is No Longer Mysticism; It Has Long Accurately Mastered Your Consumption and Life

I used to always think "big data" was a high-end industry term, far removed from ordinary people's lives.

After seeing this year's WAIC cross-industry exhibitions, I suddenly realized: big data has long permeated our daily lives, quietly mastering everyone's consumption habits and life details.

It immediately pushes exclusive offers, accurately turning your "laziness" into orders.

In the future, there will never be useless data, only people who don't know how to use it. Whoever can solve problems and match needs using detailed data will possess the fairest money-making track for ordinary people.

05 The Service Industry Is Completely Changing: The Era of Making Money by Relying on Manual Labor and Grinding Hours Is Coming to an End

This means: the service industry has officially entered the "equipment money-making era."

In the future, when opening a store or providing services, it will no longer solely rely on hiring and retaining people. Basic and repetitive work will be handed over to AI devices, while human labor will only focus on high-end customization, emotional empathy, and complex decision-making. The money-making method of simply relying on physical strength and grinding hours is being gradually eliminated.

06 AI Is No Longer Just a Chat Tool; It Has Become an All-Around Work Assistant Available to Everyone

But the AI agents comprehensively iterated by the tech giants this year have undergone a disruptive upgrade: from a single chat box, they have transformed into an all-around workstation for ordinary people, everyday professionals, and small-scale entrepreneurs.

It no longer requires you to give manual instructions step by step; it can independently understand goals, break down tasks, call tools, and deliver in a closed loop.

Reviewing contracts for risks, doing career planning, organizing work plans, designing posters and videos, editing materials—AI can handle it all in a one-stop shop.

Machines take over all the heaviest, most tiring, most dangerous, and most repetitive work for us; humans retain the core abilities of thinking, judging, creating, and empathizing.

The MIT 2025 "The GenAI Divide" report surveyed over 300 AI projects across more than 300 enterprises, with these sampled companies investing a combined $30-40 billion. The survey reveals that 95% of the projects have failed to produce measurable business returns.

You might think this kind of reference data is already outdated. Actually, it's not. The Writer 2026 AI Content Marketing Survey shows: 59% of surveyed enterprises have invested over $1 million in AI, but only 29% have seen significant business returns. The IDC Future of Work 2026 report points out: by 2026, 50% of AI use cases will fail to meet expected ROI targets.

The more money spent, the less the return.

Where's the Problem?

It’s not that the models aren't good enough; it's that the way you're using them isn't.

Based on my practical observations from working with a large number of enterprises, the vast majority of AI projects fail for the exact same reason.

Over the past couple of years, I've worked with quite a few companies and noticed a common phenomenon:

Every company has a few AI projects up and running—intelligent customer service, smart quality inspection, intelligent production scheduling... The names sound great, and the PowerPoint presentations are polished.

But ask them, "How much money have these projects made the company?" and they fall silent.

It's not that there are no results; it's that the results can't be quantified.

Intelligent customer service reduced inquiry volume by 20%, but the headcount for human agents hasn't dropped at all, because complex issues still require human intervention.

Intelligent production scheduling saved two hours, but the schedulers are still working overtime every day because plan changes are too frequent.

Every project has its "preliminary results," but not a single one has transformed the business process.

This is exactly the kind of failure the MIT report describes: not a technical failure, but an integration failure.

95% of Enterprises Have Fallen into the Same Trap

The MIT report hits the nail on the head regarding this issue:

The core of the failure is not technology, but integration. Companies are adopting AI for the sake of AI, without embedding it into their processes or solving real problems.

In plain English: you're treating AI like a toy.

You bought a hammer and are looking everywhere for nails. You see others building intelligent customer service, so you build it too. You see others deploying digital workers, so you deploy them too. But you never stop to think:

What specific business problem is this AI going to solve? Once it's solved, how will the process change? How will roles be adjusted? How will KPIs be revised?

There are no answers.

The POC (Proof of Concept, essentially an AI pilot test) is done, the results look pretty good, and then what? Then there is no "then." Dozens of POC reports sit in folders, looking great on paper, but failing to grow into actual business capabilities.

That Table Is Worth a Close Look

By now, you might be wondering: what exactly did that 5% of successful companies do right?

Dimension95% of Enterprises with Subpar Returns5% of Enterprises that Realized AI Value
Project Starting Point"We need to use AI""We need to solve a specific business problem"
POC Pilot StatusMany and scattered, with isolated projectsFew and focused, all aligned with a unified business goal
Process IntegrationAI is AI, business processes are business processesAI is embedded in the business, and processes are redesigned around AI
Performance MetricsOnly looking at "technical metrics, such as accuracy improvements"Looking at real business outcomes: cost reduction / revenue growth
Organizational & Personnel AdjustmentsOrganizational structure remains unchanged, AI used merely as an auxiliary toolRoles of humans and AI are redefined to match the new processes
Long-term PlanningPlaying it by ear, no top-level blueprintClear AI roadmap, with POCs serving the overall business blueprint

The core difference comes down to one sentence: failing companies treat AI as a tool, while successful companies treat AI as part of the process.

Tools can be bought, but processes must be changed. Changing processes means restructuring the organization, revising KPIs, and reallocating interests. This is ten times harder than just buying a model.

The Solution: From "Bonsai" to "Forest"

AI is not a one-off project; it's a continuously operated capability.

Just like buying an ERP system—you can't just buy it without implementing it. It requires configuration, training, iteration, and maintenance.

AI is no different. Deployment is just the beginning; what follows includes:

Data quality monitoring (garbage in, garbage out)

Model performance tracking (accurate today, not necessarily tomorrow)

Continuous process optimization (bottlenecks will shift, AI needs to adapt accordingly)

Organizational adaptation and iteration (the division of labor between humans and AI requires continuous fine-tuning)

Without ongoing operations, there are no returns.

IBM's research corroborates this: only 25% of AI initiatives deliver expected returns, and the common denominator among this 25% is integrating AI into core workflows, rather than treating it as an auxiliary tool.

Three Criteria for Assessment

If you're considering investing in AI, or have already invested but haven't seen a return, answer these three questions first:

Is your AI project solving a "pain point" or an "itch point"?

A pain point means "we lose money if we don't solve it," while an itch point means "it looks cool if we solve it."

Are your POCs isolated or interconnected?

A bunch of isolated POCs sitting in folders are just bonsai trees; multiple POCs pointing toward the same business goal can grow into a forest. Isolation produces bonsai, while interconnection produces a forest.

When measuring AI effectiveness, are you using "technical metrics" or "business metrics"?

"95% accuracy" is a technical metric. "Saving $300,000 in labor costs per month" is a business metric. The board of directors doesn't look at accuracy; they look at profit.

One Last Thing

The reason 95% of enterprises see no return on their AI investments is not because AI doesn't work, but because companies aren't yet ready to let AI truly deliver.

Ever thought about why, with the same AI tools, some people can operate like an entire team on their own, while you just use it to write weekly reports?

The difference is simple: you're fetching water, while they're lighting a fire.

Today, we won't dwell on empty macro concepts. Let's just talk about how to leverage these 140 billion "shadow employees" to run your business.

I. Look Beyond the Interface, Focus on the Intent

I've been grinding in the real economy for 30 years and seen countless technological shifts. But this time is different.

In the coming years, the number of active Agents in the Chinese market will reach tens of billions, or even hundreds of billions. This isn't just a numbers game; it's a complete paradigm shift in how we interact.

We used to use GUIs, where humans had to adapt to machines—clicking icons, finding menus, swiping through apps. Now we have IUIs (Intent User Interfaces): you state your intent, and the machine does the legwork.

These 140 billion Agents don't draw salaries, don't need social security, and don't need to be fed grand visions. As long as your instructions are precise and the computing power keeps up, they are a super-execution layer online 24/7.

If you're still grinding away at standardized skills that can be written into an SOP, to be honest, you're not far from being managed by the system.

II. The Power Shift: From "People Chasing Tasks" to "Tasks Chasing People"

Many people treat AI as a high-end search engine, which severely limits its potential. AI is already taking over the first half of the decision-making process.

In the past, doing business meant searching for suppliers yourself, comparing prices, and nitpicking contract terms. In the future, it's "services seeking people." Once your Agent understands your intent, it will negotiate, compare prices, and generate proposals with thousands of external Agents, ultimately presenting the optimal solution right on your desk.

In this game, traditional traffic tactics will fail, and trust will become the hard currency.

Those who only do the work will be dispatched by the system as mere resources. The real bosses are those who can define intent and make the final call.

III. The "One-Person Company" Isn't a Dream, It's a Law of Economics

Why is now the best time to start a one-person company? In the old economic parlance, it's Coase's theorem: the boundaries of a firm are determined by transaction costs.

In the past, transaction costs were high—finding people was hard, communication was exhausting, and supervision was a hassle, so you had to build a large company and hire a bunch of people to divide the labor. Now? AI has driven the costs of communication, search, and supervision down to rock bottom.

A clear-headed individual, paired with a highly executable network of Agents, can do the work that used to require hundreds of people.

This isn't some new concept; it's the inevitable result of a changed cost structure.

IV. Beware of Your Knowledge Base Becoming a "Digital Graveyard"

I've seen too many bosses spend a fortune building knowledge bases, only for them to become "digital graveyards" that no one looks at. The data is piled as high as a mountain, yet when you ask the AI, it still gives irrelevant answers.

This is the classic "fetching water" mindset—treating knowledge like water to be poured into a bucket. That's an industrial-era way of thinking.

In an era where Agents are everywhere, standardized knowledge is no longer a moat. AI calculates materials, logistics, and parameters far more accurately than you can. If all you sell are these parameterizable things, you'll soon be swallowed by the algorithm's "efficiency black box."

Your true value lies in what cannot be parameterized: the intuitive judgment based on 30 years of experience, insight into the undercurrents of your industry, and the courage to take responsibility for the outcome.

V. Three Practical Tips for Industry Veterans

If you want to prop up your "one-person company," stop learning outdated management jargon. Try these three moves:

Move One: Learn to "set the questions," don't just focus on "answering them."

AI is best at finding answers; your job is to define the problem. Define it right, and hundreds of Agents will naturally fan out, do the work, and feed the results back to you.

Move Two: Set the rules. Delegate authority, but don't relinquish control.

Today's technology already allows Agents to make payments and sign contracts on your behalf. You need to learn to use the ACT protocol and the KYA framework to draw clear red lines for AI: what it can do, what requires approval, and ensuring every transaction is traceable. You are the master; it is not.

Move Three: Turn ad-hoc operations into "compounding assets."

Don't just use AI to put out fires. Leverage infrastructure like Token Pay to manage your computing resources, build a closed-loop Agent team for continuous output, rather than disbanding after each gig.

AI won't replace you, but those who can ignite themselves and skillfully harness these 140 billion Agents will leave you so far behind you won't even see their taillights.

Don't be the "water bucket" desperately trying to fetch water. Be the match.
